text: Here's the catch. Days before Britain joined, East and West Germany reunited. Rebuilding
the East cost enormous sums, and German money started growing too fast. By July 1992, German
money supply was running around 9%, against a target of 3.5 to 5.5. So the Bundesbank
did what it always did. It raised rates. The discount rate went to 8.75%. The Lombard
rate sat at 9.75. For Germany, that made sense. For Britain, it was a disaster. Britain was in a
recession. Homeowners were drowning. Lenders repossessed about 75,000 homes in 1991 and
nearly 69,000 more in 1992. By the end of 1992, somewhere between 1 and 2 million households
owed more than their homes were worth. And here's the cruel part. The peg was working.
By the summer of 1992, British inflation was down to 3.6%. The medicine had done its job.
But Britain couldn't stop taking it. Britain needed cheaper money, but with the pound pinned
near its floor, it couldn't cut rates without the pound sinking through it. Its interest
Straits were now set, in effect, by a central bank in Frankfurt, worrying about Berlin.
That's the mirage in this story.
A fixed exchange rate looks like a fact.
It isn't.
It's a promise, and it only holds while someone is willing and able to defend it.
So, the price on me is just a promise?
You keep discovering that.
Across the Atlantic, someone was watching that promise very closely.
George Soros ran the Quantum Fund in New York. Day to day it was managed by
Stanley Druckenmiller and by most accounts the pound trade was his idea.
Here's how you bet against a currency. You borrow pounds and immediately sell
them for Deutsche Marks at around 278. If the pound later falls to say 250 you
buy those pounds back cheaper, return what you borrowed and keep the
difference. Now look at the odds. The pound was sitting near its floor. If
The pound could only rise a little, so the bet loses a little.
If Britain broke, the pound could fall a long way, and the bet wins big.
Heads, you lose a little.
Tails, you win a lot.
Traders dream of a bet like that.
But wait, isn't the Bank of England unbeatable?
It can print as many pounds as it likes.
Here's the problem.
To hold up the pound, it has to buy pounds and pay for them in other currencies like
Deutsche Marks and dollars.
Those come from its reserves, and the Bank of England can't print a single
Deutschmark. Its pockets are deep, but they have a bottom. And Soros had a
hunch about Germany. Economic historian Aylin Naeth found that Soros met
Bundesbank president Helmut Schlesinger in Basel and came away convinced the
lira and the pound would soon fall. Germany, he reckoned, would not bend to
save them. Ooh, a man who reads the room! Can he stop reading it?
